L2: # Clinical Trials
L3: ### Welcome to a resource for information on current research trials in veterinary oncology.
L4: 
L5: Pet owners often ask us if we are aware of any CLINICAL TRIALS that may be available to their cat or dog who has been diagnosed with cancer. While there certainly are a number of studies occurring around the world, participation in a clinical trial can often be difficult, especially if the trial is going on in a hospital or clinic far away from your home.
L6: Each clinical trial has very specific qualifications for participation that include everything from the breed and age of the participant to the life expectancy, weight and of course the type of cancer. Each study is very particular in its criteria for participation. Something else to take into consideration is that clinical trials are NOT always free.
L7: There may be fees to participate because grants may only cover a certain portion of the trial, and you may have to travel a long way to participate for several weeks or months perhaps.
L8: The following links represent an organized effort to provide general practitioners and their pet owners access to information to trials being conducted across the United States and, in some cases, in other countries.

L92: ## Clinical Research Trial Overview
L93: Clinical trials may involve novel diagnostic methods or therapies including chemotherapy, radiation therapy, surgical procedures, hypo- or hyperthermia, immunotherapy and photodynamic therapy, among others. While most clinical research trials are conducted at colleges of veterinary medicine, a growing number of specialty referral practices are participating in clinical research.
L94: For some trials, all visits must occur at the trials institution or practice, but for others there are tests or procedures that could be performed at the general practice.
L95: When discussing the possibility of participating in a clinical trial with pet owners, it is helpful to share that although “experimental,” or “investigational,” the safety and efficacy of new therapies and procedures have often been evaluated first in laboratory animals as well as normal dogs or cats, and the therapy is considered to be of potential benefit to the patient.
L96: 
L97: 【42†Image: Dr. Sarah Sheafor】
L98: ### Reminder for veterinarians managing pets enrolled in clinical trials
L99: Adherence to the treatment protocol is of vital importance to ensure that the protocol is followed as planned, such that the results are both reliable and meaningful. Any deviation in the pet’s health or management (including medications and supplements) must be reported to the trials institution. For most trials, owners are asked to agree to a necropsy in the event of the death of their pet. Pet owners also may appreciate the translational value of the research in which their pet may be participating.
L100: Many naturally-occurring cancers in pet animals closely resemble human cancer and provide meaningful systems for cancer research to benefit both man and animals.
L101: The clinical trials listed on this website are not run under the auspices of the Veterinary Cancer Society. Clinical trials are performed in order to assess the toxicity and/or efficacy of a certain treatment protocol. While the hope is that the investigators will find a less toxic or more effective treatment for cancer, there are no guarantees regarding the outcome of any trials listed on clinical searchable database found on this site.

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating experimental antiviral treatments for cats diagnosed with feline infectious peritonitis (FIP), including both the effusive (“wet”) and non-effusive (“dry”) forms of the disease.

FIP is a serious viral disease caused by feline coronavirus (FCoV). Researchers are studying different treatment options to better understand their safety and effectiveness in cats with FIP.

Cats enrolled in the study may receive different experimental antiviral treatments depending on the needs of the patient and study protocol. Cats will be closely monitored throughout the study period to evaluate response to treatment and overall health.
current_roster.tagline: New Hope for FIP
current_roster.name: New Treatments for FIP (Feline Infectious Peritonitis)

current_roster.description: This study is for dogs that have bladder cancer called transitional cell carcinoma (TCC). The goal is to find out if using radiation therapy together with a pill called lapatinib is safe and well‑tolerated by dogs. Researchers will watch closely for side effects and see how dogs respond to the treatment over about 4 months.
current_roster.tagline: Help us study canine bladder translational cell carcinoma.
current_roster.name: Combination of Lapatinib and Fractionated Radiation Therapy for Dogs with Transitional Cell Carcinoma

current_roster.description:
This study looks at how a medicine called rapamycin affects aging and health in dogs. Rapamycin has helped mice live longer and stay healthier as they age. The goal of the TRIAD (Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs) study is to see if rapamycin can help dogs stay healthier as they get older, especially with their heart, movement, and brain function.

Researchers want to learn if rapamycin can:

  1. Improve heart health
  2. Help dogs move more easily
  3. Help dogs think and remember better as they age
  4. Possibly help dogs live longer
current_roster.tagline: Help us study how a medication can improve health and lifespan in aging dogs.
current_roster.name: The Dog Aging Project: Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD)

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new type of cancer treatment called CAR T cell therapy for dogs with osteosarcoma that has spread to the lungs.

CAR T cell therapy uses your dog’s own immune cells to help fight cancer. A blood sample is collected (about 3-4 tablespoons), and special immune cells (called T cells) are modified in a lab to better recognize and attack cancer cells. These upgraded cells are then given back to your dog through an IV infusion.

Dogs in this study will also receive medications to prepare the body for treatment and to support the immune system during the study. The goal is to determine if this treatment is safe and effective for dogs with metastatic bone cancer.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test a new treatment for advanced bone cancer in dogs.
current_roster.name: CAR T Cell Immunotherapy for Metastatic Osteosarcoma in Dogs

current_roster.description: Local lymph nodes are a common site for the cancer to spread in dogs with anal sac tumors. A safe and common test to find the lymph nodes that drain fluid from a tumor is sentinel lymph node (SLN) mapping. However, the lymph nodes that drain anal sac tumors are located within the abdomen and pelvis, which means that SLN mapping in dogs with anal sac tumors has needed open abdominal surgery. Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has many reported benefits for patients compared to open abdominal surgery, including smaller incisions, reduced pain, and earlier return to function. The goal of this study is to evaluate SLN mapping techniques via a MIS approach in dogs with anal sac tumors and compare the results to other methods.
current_roster.tagline: Finding draining lymph nodes for anal gland tumors in dogs using minimally invasive surgery
current_roster.name: Minimally invasive sentinel lymph node mapping for dogs with anal sac adenocarcinoma (AGASACA)

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a non-surgical chemotherapy treatment for dogs with brain tumors, particularly gliomas, which are one of the most common and difficult types to treat.

The goal is to test a chemotherapy drug called verdinexor, which may be more effective at targeting these tumors without the need for brain surgery. This treatment is given orally and aims to slow tumor growth and improve outcomes.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test verdinexor, a new chemotherapy for brain tumors in dogs.
current_roster.name: Non-surgical Chemotherapy Treatment for Canine Brain Tumors

current_roster.description:
Feline Lower Urinary Tract Disease (FLUTD) is a common condition that affects many young cats. It can cause frequent trips to the litter box, straining to urinate, blood in the urine, and pain during urination. In male cats, FLUTD can sometimes lead to a complete urinary blockage, which is a life-threatening emergency.

While diet changes and reducing stress may help lower the risk of future blockages, there is currently no cure for FLUTD, and many cats experience repeat urinary blockages.

This study is evaluating whether low-dose radiation therapy can safely reduce inflammation and help prevent future urinary blockages in male cats with FLUTD. Early results from another veterinary hospital have been encouraging, with most treated cats avoiding future blockages after treatment. Researchers hope this treatment can improve quality of life while reducing the need for repeated hospitalizations.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluating a new treatment to reduce repeat urinary blockages in male cats with feline lower urinary tract disease.
current_roster.name: Low-Dose Radiation Therapy for Cats with Urinary Blockage (FLUTD)

current_roster.description:
This study looks at the best way to treat immune‑mediated hemolytic anemia (IMHA) in cats. IMHA is a disease where a cat’s own immune system attacks its red blood cells, causing anemia (low red blood cell counts).

The study compares two treatments:

  1. Prednisolone alone (a steroid)
  2. Atopica (an immune‑suppressing medication)

The goal is to see which treatment works better and is safer for cats with IMHA.
current_roster.tagline: Join our study comparing two treatment options for cats with IMHA.
current_roster.name: Treatment of Immune-Mediated Anemia (IMHA) in Cats
current_roster.study_type: Clinical Trial for Immune-Mediated Anemia in Cats

current_roster.description: This study looks at whether a chemotherapy drug called carboplatin can help reduce pain in dogs that have osteosarcoma (bone cancer) in a leg. The researchers want to see if this medication improves how well dogs walk, how active they are during the day, and how well they sleep after treatment.
current_roster.tagline: Help us study how carboplatin can help manage pain in dogs with bone cancer.
current_roster.name: Effect of Intravenous Carboplatin on Pain Control in Dogs with Appendicular Osteosarcoma

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to test a new immunotherapy treatment that is injected directly into the tumor. Researchers want to find out how well the treatment works and how safe it is in cats.
current_roster.tagline: Help Investigate a novel immunotherapy for cats with oral squamous cell carcinoma
current_roster.name: Novel Immunotherapy for Cats with Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma

current_roster.description: This pilot study looks at whether a steroid medicine called triamcinolone can help dogs with osteoarthritis feel better. The steroid is given as a shot into a muscle, opposed to directly into the joint. The goal is to see if this reduces limping, lowers joint pain, and evaluate the safety and efficacy of the steroid. This type of treatment has helped people, so veterinarians and researchers want to see if it is also safe and helpful for dogs.
current_roster.tagline: Join our research on using a steroid injection to reduce pain and improve mobility in dogs.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of triamcinolone for osteoarthritis in dogs
current_roster.study_type: Clinical Trial for Dogs with Osteoarthritis
current_roster.top_investigator: Felix Duerr, DVM, MS, DACVS-SA, DECVS, DACVSMR

current_roster.description:
This study is to investigate different treatment protocols in the treatment for copper-associated chronic hepatitis in dogs. Eligible dogs would include dogs that have been diagnosed by liver biopsy with this disease and have not yet started a low copper diet or have received chelation therapy (e.g. D-penicillamine). Exclusion criteria includes if dogs have not been biopsied and diagnosed with this disease and if they are receiving drugs that can affect their immune system.


This is a 6 month long trial where blood work, urine testing, and laparoscopic liver biopsies at 6 months are all covered by the trial. These rechecks are not in addition to the standard rechecks we would normally pursue in any patient affected by this disease.
current_roster.tagline: Help us investigate new treatment options for dogs with copper-associated liver disease.
current_roster.name: Join Our Study on Copper-Associated Chronic Hepatitis in Dogs

current_roster.description: The adrenal glands are small organs in the abdomen that secrete hormones important for normal body function. Adrenal disease is very common in ferrets and affects roughly 25-70% of the North American population. This study’s goal is to establish guidelines for CT scans that could give us better visualization (and therefore information) of adrenal glands. This study will enroll healthy ferrets and ferrets with suspected adrenal disease for full-body CT scans and ultrasounds of their adrenal glands.
current_roster.tagline: Helping improve the diagnosis of adrenal disease in ferrets through advanced imaging techniques
current_roster.name: CT Imaging Study for Ferret Adrenal Disease

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new treatment approach for dogs with immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (IMTP), a serious autoimmune disease that causes the immune system to destroy platelets. Very low platelet counts can increase the risk of severe or life-threatening bleeding.

Current treatment for IMTP often includes steroids and other immune-suppressing medications, but these treatments may take several days to improve platelet counts. This study will evaluate a rapid steroid induction protocol using high doses of intravenous methylprednisolone to determine whether it can induce remission more quickly while remaining safe and well tolerated.

Researchers will also evaluate how this treatment affects the immune system using blood samples collected during the study.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluating a high-dose steroid protocol to help dogs with IMTP achieve remission more quickly.
current_roster.name: Rapid Steroid Treatment for Dogs with Immune-Mediated Thrombocytopenia
current_roster.top_investigator: Charles Talbot, BVSc, MS, MANZCVS (ECC), DACVECC

current_roster.description:
This study is focused on better understanding ductal plate malformations, which are congenital (present at birth) liver conditions that affect the bile ducts in dogs and cats. Examples include von Meyenburg complex, congenital hepatic fibrosis, and Caroli disease.

Right now, very little is known about how these diseases progress over time, and there are no clear guidelines for the best treatment. The goal of this study is to follow pets with this condition and learn more about their long-term health and outcomes.

This is an observational study, meaning your pet’s treatment will be decided by your veterinarian, not the study. Researchers will collect information over time to better understand the disease and improve care in the future.
current_roster.tagline: Help us understand long-term outcomes for cats and dogs with ductal plate malformations.
current_roster.name: Clinical Characteristics and Long-Term Outcome in Cats and Dogs Diagnosed with Ductal Plate Malformation

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new type of cancer treatment for dogs with soft tissue sarcoma. The treatment uses your dog’s own immune cells (called T cells) to help fight cancer.

A blood sample is collected (about 3-4 tablespoons), and the T cells are modified in a lab to better recognize and attack cancer cells. These upgraded cells (called CAR T cells) are then given back to your dog through an IV infusion.

Dogs in this study may also receive oral immunotherapy medications to help improve how well the treatment works.

The goal of this study is to determine if this treatment is safe and effective in dogs with soft tissue sarcoma.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test a new combination therapy for soft tissue sarcoma in dogs.
current_roster.name: Clinical Testing of Canine T Cells Engineered to Target Soft Tissue Sarcoma with Oral Immunotherapy

current_roster.description:
This study is for dogs that have cancer. Veterinarians and researchers want to see if common vaccines can be repurposed to help a dog’s immune system fight cancer. Dogs in the study will be randomly chosen to receive either vaccines normally used for people (Shingrix or Gardasil) or a rabies vaccine.


At first, dogs will receive 1 to 3 weekly vaccine injections to boost immune response. After that, they will receive weekly injections directly into the tumor for 8 weeks. During the study, doctors will collect small samples from the tumor and nearby lymph nodes at certain times to see how the cancer is responding. Blood samples will also be taken at each visit. The clinical and research team will closely watch how each dog’s tumor changes during treatment.
current_roster.tagline: COTC033: Help us test a new approach to treat cancer by using vaccine immunity in dogs.
current_roster.name: Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers in Dogs

current_roster.description:
This study is looking at the connection between feline plasma cell pododermatitis (FPP) and kidney disease in cats. FPP is a condition that causes the paw pads to become swollen, discolored, cracked, and sometimes ulcerated.


Researchers have found that some cats with FPP may also develop a serious type of autoimmune kidney disease called immune complex mediated glomerulonephritis (ICGN). ICGN can cause significant illness and may shorten a cat’s lifespan if not diagnosed and treated early.


The goal of this study is to better understand how often cats with FPP develop kidney disease and how these cats respond to treatment over time. Cats enrolled in the study will be monitored over a 2-year period using bloodwork and urine testing to look for early signs of kidney disease.
current_roster.tagline: A long-term study evaluating the connection between plasma cell pododermatitis and kidney disease in cats
current_roster.name: Studying Kidney Disease in Cats with Paw Pad Disease

current_roster.description:
This study, “Evaluation of autologous protein solution as an anti-inflammatory therapeutic for adult horses with naturally occurring lameness isolated to the medial femorotibial joint,” is sponsored by Zoetis, LLC and supported by the Orthopaedic Research Center and Equine Sports Medicine Service at the CSU Johnson Family Equine Hospital.


The purpose of this study is to compare two different treatments for horses with stifle joint lameness: autologous protein solution [APS (Prostride)] versus a corticosteroid and hyaluronic acid (HA) injection.


Horses enrolled in the study will receive lameness exams, x-rays, ultrasound and treatment of the affected stifle at no cost, plus a financial incentive upon completion of the 24-week study. Owners and veterinarians will not know which treatment the horse receives during the study.
current_roster.tagline: A study evaluating two different treatments (steroids vs an orthobiologic) for horses with stifle joint lameness
current_roster.name: Comparing Treatments for Stifle Lameness in Horses

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate ketamine infusion therapy as a treatment for chronic pain associated with coffin or pastern joint osteoarthritis in horses. Ketamine infusions are used to provide long term pain relief for chronic conditions in humans. While these infusions are frequently used to treat acute or post-surgical pain in horses, their long term effect in horses with chronic pain has not been established.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluating a novel treatment to provide longer-lasting pain relief for horses with coffin and pastern joint arthritis.
current_roster.name: Ketamine Infusion Therapy for Horses with Chronic Arthritis Pain

current_roster.description:
Canine transmissible venereal tumor (TVT) is an infectious cancer that can be spread between dogs, often through grooming behaviors or sexual contact. This cancer can be found worldwide, but is most common in Central and South America, Africa, and Asia. In the United States, this cancer is most commonly seen in animals rescued from other parts of the world, or in free-roaming pets in very remote areas.


Treatment for this cancer involves once-weekly injections of chemotherapy, which are given until the cancer is resolved. For patients who cannot undergo this chemotherapy treatment, finding alternate therapies can be invaluable. We know that this cancer responds well to older forms of radiation therapy; however, we aim to determine if a single treatment with modernized radiation can provide similar treatment outcomes with fewer visits compared to chemotherapy.
current_roster.name: Single Radiation Treatment for Dogs with Transmissible Venereal Tumor

current_roster.description: The goal of this study is to evaluate the ability of a specific stem cell product to alleviate symptoms associated with arthritis in dogs. This stem cell product is a proprietary ‘allogeneic stromal cell treatment’, which means that it contains stem cells collected from a donor dog. The procedure of using cells from a donor dog (“allogeneic” cells) has been utilized in several other research studies (including research performed here at CSU using cells produced at CSU). However, this is the first study at CSU using this specific stem cell product.
current_roster.tagline: Help us evaluate a stem cell therapy for dogs with arthritis.
current_roster.name: Join Our Study Testing a New Stem Cell Treatment for Canine Osteoarthritis
current_roster.top_investigator: Felix Duerr, DVM, MS, DACVS-SA, DECVS, DACVSMR

current_roster.description:
About 3 in 100 dogs are diagnosed with brain tumors each year, and gliomas are among the hardest to treat because they can escape traditional treatments. This study is focused on finding new treatment options for dogs with brain tumors, specifically gliomas, which are one of the most difficult types to treat. Researchers are exploring a new approach called immunotherapy, which helps the body’s own immune system fight cancer.


In this study, a small blood sample is taken from your dog to collect immune cells (called T cells). These cells are then modified in the lab to better recognize and attack cancer cells. The upgraded cells (called CAR T cells) are given back to your dog to target the tumor.


Dogs in this study will also receive a chemotherapy drug called verdinexor, which may help improve the effectiveness of the treatment.


Additionally, dogs can receive radiation therapy, which is currently the gold-standard for treating gliomas in dogs. We hope that by attacking the tumor through immunotherapy, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy, we will give dogs the best chance at success.


This is the first study to test this type of therapy in dogs, building on promising results seen in children with brain tumors.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test CAR T cells and verdinexor, a new chemotherapy for gliomas in dogs.
current_roster.name: Immunotherapy (CAR-T) treatment for canine glioma tumors

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new topical anti-inflammatory gel (Tat-PYC-Smad7) for dogs with atopic dermatitis (environmental allergies). Many dogs with environmental allergies need topical treatments in addition to their regular medications to help control skin inflammation and itching.

Tat-PYC-Smad7 has previously been used in dogs and mice to treat inflammatory oral lesions and has shown reduced inflammation and improved healing. This study will evaluate whether the gel can safely reduce skin inflammation associated with atopic dermatitis.

The study is double-blinded, meaning neither owners nor veterinarians will know which skin lesion is receiving the active treatment and which is receiving the placebo gel during the study.
current_roster.tagline: Evaluating a new anti-inflammatory gel to help reduce skin inflammation in dogs with atopic dermatitis.
current_roster.name: Investigational Topical Gel for Dogs with Environmental Allergies

current_roster.description:
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a fast-growing cancer of the blood and bone marrow that affects both people and dogs. Dogs diagnosed with AML usually have a poor outlook, and current treatments only extend survival for a short time, typically about 1–2 months.

Researchers are looking for better treatment options for dogs with AML. Many dogs with AML have changes (mutations) in a gene called NRAS, which can cause cancer cells to grow and survive. This study is testing a medication called trametinib, which blocks signals that cancer cells use to grow.

The purpose of this study is to find out whether trametinib is safe for dogs with AML and whether it may help slow down or reduce the cancer. Information learned from this study may also help researchers better understand leukemia in people.

This trial is being led by the Clinical Hematopathology Laboratory in partnership with the Flint Animal Cancer Center of the Colorado State University Veterinary Health System and is sponsored by the Lutsen Linder Research Fund for Extremely Gorgeous Dogs.
current_roster.tagline: Help investigate new ways to battle acute myeloid leukemia!
current_roster.name: Pilot clinical trial of anti-cancer therapy with trametinib in naturally occurring acute myeloid leukemia

current_roster.description:
Epilepsy is the most common brain disorder in dogs and affects up to 1 in 20 dogs. Many seizure medications can cause unwanted side effects, so there is a need for other treatment options. This study will test a special diet to see if it can help reduce seizures without adding more medication.


This study is looking for dogs that are currently taking at least one anti-seizure medication and still have at least 1 seizure every 2 months. There are two groups in this study:


  1. Group 1 is for dogs that have 2 or more seizures each month. Dogs in this group will first complete a baseline period of up to 3 months, or until they have had 5 separate seizures. After that, they will spend 6 months eating either the test diet or a high-quality maintenance diet.
  2. Group 2 is for dogs that have 1–2 seizures every 2 months. Dogs in this group will first complete a baseline period of up to 6 months, or until they have had 3 separate seizures. After that, they will spend 12 months eating either the test diet or a high-quality maintenance diet. Dogs doing well in the study may be offered an extra 6 months on the study diet.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test a special diet to reduce seizures in dogs without extra medication.
current_roster.name: The Effect of a Novel Diet on Epilepsy in Dogs

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new immunotherapy treatment for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) affecting the eye and surrounding tissues in horses, including the eyelids and ocular surface.

SCC is the most common tumor affecting the eye in horses. The goal of this study is to determine if a novel immunotherapy injection can safely reduce tumor size or lead to remission.

Horses enrolled in the study will receive injections of the immunotherapy while standing under sedation. Tumor size and response to treatment will be monitored throughout the study.
current_roster.tagline: Join our study testing a new Immunotherapy for the treatment of eyelid and corneolimbal squamous cell carcinoma in horses
current_roster.name: New Immunotherapy Treatment for Eye Cancer in Horses

current_roster.description:
Diabetes is a common disease in both cats and people. While we know that people with diabetes are more likely to develop tendon injuries that can cause pain and limping, we do not yet know if the same is true for cats.

This study aims to better understand whether cats with diabetes develop changes to the Achilles tendon that may contribute to pain and mobility problems. Researchers will examine tissue samples collected after a cat has passed away to better understand how diabetes affects tendons and other tissues. This information may help veterinarians recognize and treat pain associated with diabetes in future feline patients.
current_roster.tagline: Donate tissue samples to help improve the diagnosis and treatment of diabetic cats.
current_roster.name: Helping Researchers Better Understand Diabetes in Cats

current_roster.description:
This study is focused on improving treatment options for brain tumors in dogs and cats. While progress has been made, many types of brain tumors still have limited treatment options.

The goal of this study is to collect tumor samples to better understand different types of brain cancer. These samples are shared with researchers at CSU and partner institutions around the world. This work may help develop new treatments not only for pets, but also for people with brain cancer.

Your pet’s participation can help advance research and contribute to future breakthroughs in both veterinary and human medicine.
current_roster.tagline: Help us advance brain tumor treatments for pets and humans.
current_roster.name: Biorepository and Advanced Research in Brain Cancer (BARC)

current_roster.description: Urothelial carcinoma (UC) is the most common type of bladder cancer in dogs. For dogs with tumors in certain locations, surgical removal (partial cystectomy) can improve outcomes with low risk. New minimally invasive techniques that maintain a closed bladder may offer additional benefits and warrant further investigation, but these approaches currently rely on specialized camera equipment within the bladder, which is not always available, to identify tumors. This pilot study will test whether a safe dye, indocyanine green (ICG), used with near-infrared (NIR) imaging can identify bladder tumors and their edges during surgery. The findings with NIR will be compared with what is seen by the surgeon and with microscopic examination by a pathologist. Results will be incorporated into future studies with novel surgical techniques that have the potential to improve outcomes in dogs with UC.
current_roster.tagline: Using a Fluorescent Dye to Identify Bladder Tumors in Dogs During Surgery
current_roster.name: Near-Infrared Fluorescence Imaging with Indocyanine Green for Intraoperative Detection of Canine Urothelial Carcinoma

current_roster.description: Sarcoids are the most common type of skin tumor found in horses. Right now, there is no treatment that works the same way for every horse. This study is testing a new, experimental treatment to see if it can safely make sarcoids go away (called remission) or at least make them much smaller. All horses in the study will receive the same treatment, which is an injection of an immunotherapy. This treatment is still being studied, so it is not yet known how well it works or how safe it is. The study includes physical exams, blood draws, photos, and injections every 4 weeks for 3 visits, with follow-up appointments at 1 month, 3 months and 6 months post injection series.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test a new treatment for sarcoids, the most common skin tumor in horses.
current_roster.name: Evaluation of a New Immunotherapy for Sarcoids in Horses
current_roster.study_type: Clinical Trial for Sarcoids in Horses

current_roster.description:
One of the most lacking areas in veterinary medicine is the ability to diagnose early dementia in dogs and cats. Our team is working diligently on creating simple blood tests that we hope will be able to fulfill this need but first, we need to be able to correlate the blood tests with levels of protein found in the brain.


By collecting samples from dogs and cats who have recently passed away, we’re able to compare these blood protein levels to those of the levels in the brain itself, which should allow us to develop this test in live animals. Our hope is that we will ultimately be able to diagnose early dementia in dogs and cats before symptoms develop, allowing us to better treat the pet to give them more quality time with their family.
current_roster.tagline: Help us develop early dementia diagnostics by contributing samples from your recently deceased pet.
current_roster.name: A Lasting Legacy: Samples Collected from Pets After Death to Study Diseases of Aging

current_roster.description: This study looks at how bones change in dogs with bone cancer in the leg (called osteosarcoma) after radiation treatment. Veterinarians and researchers will test blood and urine to see how much bone is breaking down before and after a special type of radiation treatment called SBRT (stereotactic body radiation therapy). They will compare this information to bone strength, how well the treatment works, and the risk of the bone breaking.
current_roster.tagline: Help us study how radiation and chemotherapy affect bone health in dogs with bone cancer.
current_roster.name: Dual Energy CT to Assess Bone Mineral Density in Dogs with Osteosarcoma Undergoing Stereotactic Body Radiation Therapy

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new limb-sparing surgery for dogs with bone cancer (osteosarcoma). Instead of removing the limb, this approach uses a custom 3D-printed implant to replace the diseased bone.

The implant is designed specifically for your dog using advanced imaging and is made from a material that can gradually be replaced by your dog’s own bone over time. The goal is to maintain limb function while treating the cancer.

Dogs in this study will undergo surgery followed by chemotherapy and long-term monitoring to evaluate how well the implant works and how the cancer responds to treatment.
current_roster.tagline: A personalized 3D-printed implant designed to replace bone and help your dog keep their leg
current_roster.name: A Limb-Sparing Option for Bone Cancer in Dogs

current_roster.description:
A biobank is a secure facility that collects, processes, and stores blood, tissue, and other biological samples for future research.

The CSU Trauma Biobank is collecting samples from dogs and cats with traumatic injuries, as well as healthy pets, to help researchers better understand how the body responds to trauma. By studying these samples, researchers hope to improve the diagnosis and treatment of traumatic injuries in animals while also supporting research that may benefit human medicine.

Samples and health information are stored securely and de-identified before being shared with approved researchers.
current_roster.tagline: Your pet's samples can help researchers develop better diagnostics and treatments for traumatic injuries.
current_roster.name: Building the Future of Veterinary Trauma Care

visible_sc_items.tag_path: centers_Veterinary Emergency and Critical Care, Trauma, and Translational Research
visible_sc_items.label: Veterinary Emergency and Critical Care, Trauma, and Translational Research

current_roster.description:
Staggering disease is a serious illness that affects the nervous system and causes trouble walking, especially in the back legs. It has been seen in cats in Europe for more than 50 years, but it has almost never been found in the United States. In 2023, one case was found in a wild mountain lion in Colorado.

This study is looking for more cases to understand if this disease is affecting cats in the U.S. Researchers and veterinarians are asking for cats that are suspected to have staggering disease to be submitted for testing so they can learn how common it is and what causes it.
current_roster.tagline: Help us investigate the presence of staggering disease in domestic cats across the US.
current_roster.name: Staggering Disease Surveillance Study for Cats

current_roster.description:
This study is evaluating a new immunotherapy treatment for genital squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in male horses. This type of cancer can be aggressive and may require invasive surgery if not treated early.

The goal of this study is to determine if a novel immunotherapy (LTAC) can safely reduce tumor size or lead to remission. Early research has shown promising results, with tumors shrinking after treatment and minimal side effects.

Treatment involves injecting the immunotherapy directly into the tumor to help the horse’s immune system fight the cancer.
current_roster.tagline: Join our research on immunotherapy for genital cancer in male horses.
current_roster.name: Help Us Study a New Treatment for Cancer in Horses

current_roster.description:
Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is very common in cats and can make them very sick over time. Many cats with CKD have problems like high phosphorus levels in their blood and dehydration. These problems can make cats feel tired, sick to their stomach, or lose their appetite.


Veterinarians often recommend treatments like medicines that lower phosphorus (called intestinal phosphate binders) and fluids given under the skin (subcutaneous fluids). However, there are not many studies showing how well these treatments really work. This six‑month study looks at how phosphate binders and subcutaneous fluids help cats with CKD over time.
current_roster.tagline: Help us test a new treatment for chronic kidney disease in cats
current_roster.name: Investigating the efficacy of intestinal phosphate binders and subcutaneous fluid therapy in the management of feline chronic kidney disease

current_roster.description:
The Brain Health Study is a long-term research program at Colorado State University designed to understand how dogs age and why some develop cognitive decline. Dogs aged 1 year and up are welcome to participate. Depending on your dog's age, size, health, and other factors, our team may recommend one of several research pathways. These pathways may include bloodwork, cognitive testing, owner surveys, and, for some dogs, advanced imaging studies.


Right now, there is no accurate way to diagnose early dementia in dogs, and no single treatment that works well for all cases. The goal of this study is to learn more about brain aging by comparing younger, healthy dogs to older dogs.
current_roster.tagline: Help us understand how dogs age and develop cognitive changes.
current_roster.name: Brain Health Study: Helping Dogs Live Longer, Healthier Lives

L82: # Clinical Trial Service
L83: 
L84: Clinical trials are studies that explore whether a procedure, treatment, diagnostic test, or medical device is safe and effective. Trials help answer questions, and the answers can benefit both animal and human health because of the many diseases common to both. By participating in a clinical trial, you and your pet are helping us advance the future health and well-being of animals and humans.
L85: The Lloyd Veterinary Medical Center has outstanding veterinary expertise through its board-certified clinicians, faculty, and technical staff in a state-of-the-art facility. We have expertise and experience in conducting clinical trials and analyzing the data.

current_roster.description: Collection of blood and urine samples for research purposes may allow us to better understand the causes of cancer in pets and may lead to improvements in the detection, diagnosis, and treatment of canine tumors. Additionally, evaluation of blood and urine can help us to determine efficacy of novel procedures such as prostate embolization.
current_roster.tagline: Help us collect blood and urine to study a new surgical technique!
current_roster.name: Looking at a new treatment and assessing the outcome through blood and urine in dogs with prostate cancer

current_roster.description: Megaesophagus literally means large or giant esophagus and refers to a syndrome in which the muscles of the esophagus lose their tone and are no longer able to propel food and water from the mouth into the stomach. This disease is common in large-breed dogs in particular and can occur at any age. While some other diseases can cause megaesophagus, in over 50% of dogs no underlying or treatable cause is identified (known as idiopathic-acquired megaesophagus). As such, no targeted therapy can be implemented. Few advancements have been made in recommendations for disease management with current suggestions documented to be inadequate. We are assessing esophageal and lower esophageal sphincter (LES) function to optimize management of megaesophagus (ME) using novel medical therapies.
current_roster.tagline: Help us find better ways of treating dogs with megaesophagus!
current_roster.name: Assessing and managing megaesophagus in dogs

current_roster.description:
When liver tumors in dogs cannot be removed with surgery, treatment options are limited or non-existent. In humans, one of the standard treatments for those cases is transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), which eliminates the blood supply of the tumor and may decrease tumor size. The objectives of this study are to 1) describe the procedure of TACE  using a novel treatment agent in a group of dogs with naturally-occurring liver cancer, and 2) evaluate the effect that liver TACE has on clinical signs, size and viability of the tumor.

Demonstrating the feasibility and efficacy of liver TACE to improve clinical signs and decrease tumor size and volume can significantly advance our treatment of this difficult disease process, as current treatment options are limited and lack efficacy. Additionally, liver TACE is minimally invasive and provides many potential advantages over traditional surgical therapies.
current_roster.tagline: Help us learn more about this new technique that could shrink liver tumors in dogs!
current_roster.name: Assessing a new technique to shrink liver tumors in dogs

current_roster.description:
Cancer resulting in obstruction of the lower urinary tract of dogs is most commonly found in the prostate, urinary bladder and urethra (tube responsible for draining urine out of the body). Unfortunately, cancer of the lower urinary tract often results in complete blockage of the urethra, causing a patient to be unable to pass urine. The inability to urinate is a life-threatening emergency.

The placement of urethral stents is generally performed with fluoroscopic-guidance (use of “real-time” x-rays). While fluoroscopy is useful for stent placement, there may be other techniques that could be considered. Traditionally, ultrasonographic assessment of tumor size and location has been performed by transabdominal ultrasound (where the ultrasound probe is placed on the abdominal wall to allow for visualization of organs within the abdomen), but this method can be inaccurate. The use of transrectal ultrasound (where an ultrasound probe is placed into the rectum) circumvents these previously discussed problems, and therefore, the purpose of this study is to evaluate this technique for efficacy.
current_roster.tagline: Help us study a new technique to place urethral stents in dogs with prostate, bladder, and/or urethra tumors!
current_roster.name: Surgical technique to place urethral stents in dogs with prostate, bladder and/or urethra tumors

current_roster.description:
Please note that we have many inquiries coming through for this study, with limited spaces left. We ask that you be patient as we sort through inquires and do our best to get back to each individual.

Please note we are only enrolling cats diagnosed with the DRY form of FIP at this time

Pets and their owners must reside within close proximity of Davis, CA. Before we can enroll your cat, we require a full set of veterinary records to be sent to our office by your veterinarian.

Feline infectious peritonitis (FIP) is a fatal disease of cats with no available FDA-approved treatment or vaccine. Antiviral drugs that decrease virus replication have been investigated in cats with FIP with promising results. In this trial, your cat will receive an investigational oral antiviral drug.

If you are looking for more information on current FIP treatments and news, please visit this site: https://ccah.vetmed.ucdavis.edu/cats/resources/general-feline-infectious-peritonitis-resources.
current_roster.tagline: FIP
current_roster.name: Help us assess an antiviral drug for treating FIP in cats.

current_roster.description: The CAALM Study is evaluating the safety, tolerability, and preliminary efficacy of a novel dog PDL1 antibody (UCD-PDL1). This cutting-edge trial seeks to optimize dosing while exploring the antibody’s potential to improve survival outcomes for dogs with oral melanoma that has spread to the lungs.
current_roster.tagline: Pioneering hope for dogs with metastatic cancer
current_roster.name: Innovative Immunotherapy for Canine Lung Metastases: The CAALM Study

current_roster.description:
Cats with chronic itching are often difficult to treat because there are very few safe and effective anti-itch medications available for feline patients. This study aims to better understand the biology behind moderate to severe itch in cats and support the development of new treatment options.


Researchers at the UC Davis School of Veterinary Medicine are partnering with the Scripps Research Institute to study molecules in the blood that may contribute to itching. By comparing samples from itchy cats and healthy cats, this research may help identify new targets for medications that can bring relief and improve quality of life for cats in the future.
current_roster.tagline: Advancing care and comfort for cats with allergic skin disease.
current_roster.name: Developing Better Treatments for Cats with Itchy Skin

current_roster.description:
Dogs diagnosed with glioma, an aggressive brain tumor, often experience limited benefit from standard treatments such as radiation therapy alone. This clinical trial is evaluating a novel investigational drug called bisaminoquinoline-13 (BAQ-13) that may help improve how brain tumors respond to radiation therapy.


BAQ-13 works by blocking a process called autophagy, which cancer cells use to survive treatment. This study will evaluate whether BAQ-13 can safely reach brain tumors, be tolerated by dogs receiving radiation therapy, and show early signs of effectiveness.
current_roster.tagline: A research study evaluating a novel drug alongside radiation therapy for dogs with brain tumors.
current_roster.name: CARE Trial: Combined Autophagy inhibition and Radiation therapy to improve Efficacy in Canine Glioma
current_roster.top_investigator: Christine Toedebusch, DVM, PhD, DACVIM, Associate Professor

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to compare the treatment of ear sarcoids in horses to see if the addition of photodynamic therapy (PDT) provides a lower rate of recurrence and faster healing time compared to regular laser excision. Sarcoids are the most common type of cancer identified in horses.


Tumors may be quiescent for a period of time, but most eventually become aggressive and highly invasive, extending into surrounding tissues and causing significant discomfort. Several treatment methods have been used to treat sarcoids, including surgical removal, cryotherapy, laser therapy, topical and local injectable chemotherapies, electrochemotherapy, and immunotherapy. When managing sarcoids on the ear, recurrence remains a concern, as wide tissue margins are necessary to ensure optimal outcomes. Obtaining large surgical margins in the inner and outer ears can be challenging due to the ear's contour. 


Combining photodynamic therapy (PDT) with diode laser excision may offer enhanced disease control. PDT uses light of a specific wavelength to target a dye that has been applied to the cancerous tissues and kills the cancer cells after activation with the laser. It is anticipated that the addition of PDT to diode laser tumor removal will provide better disease control (lower recurrence) and improve surgical wound healing. Sarcoid treatment that offers improved disease control and faster wound healing would be beneficial in areas that are often difficult to treat, such as the ear. If the use of PDT improves outcomes in this subset of horses, the treatment could be applied to select sarcoids in other anatomic locations.
current_roster.tagline: Ear sarcoid treatment in horses
current_roster.name: Comparing laser removal with and without photodynamic therapy for the treatment of ear sarcoids in horses
current_roster.top_investigator: Lauren Charnock, Assistant Professor of Veterinary Ophthalmology

current_roster.description:
CAR T cell therapy has fundamentally changed how certain cancers are treated. By reprogramming a patient's own T lymphocytes to express a receptor targeting a protein on tumor cells, it directs the immune system to destroy them, producing durable remissions in blood cancers once refractory to conventional treatment.


These benefits have yet to reach veterinary patients, and some cancers remain especially hard to treat with immunotherapy. Sarcomas can be very resistant to standard treatment across many species, including dogs. Led by investigators at Colorado State University, we are testing CAR T cells engineered against FAP, a protein highly expressed in many sarcomas, in pet dogs. We are evaluating both the therapy's activity and its side effects. Advancing this work meets a real clinical need for companion animals while accelerating progress for human patients as well.


In this study, we will test a new treatment for dogs with sarcomas. As the tumor has to be biopsied, this study is best for sarcomas that are external or on the outside of the body.
current_roster.tagline: New treatment with autologous FAP CAR T-cells for sarcomas
current_roster.name: Treatment of Canine Sarcoma with FAP CAR T-cells (FAP CAR-T Study)
current_roster.top_investigator: Rachel Brady, DVM, PhD, Assistant Professor

current_roster.description: Bilateral corneal stromal loss (BCSL) is a potentially progressive ocular disease that can be associated with pain, vision loss and even loss of the eye. The objective of this study is to determine the role genetics plays in BCSL in Friesian horses. This study is designed to determine the incidence of BCSL in the breed, to determine the mode of inheritance if a single gene is involved, and identify candidate genes for further investigation.
current_roster.tagline: Help us find out why Friesians are at a higher risk of getting bilateral corneal stromal loss!
current_roster.name: Understanding the genetics causing bilateral corneal stromal loss in Friesian horses

current_roster.description: Sudden acquired retinal degeneration syndrome (SARDS) is a common cause of permanent blindness in dogs. Dogs usually present with rapid onset of blindness with no obvious abnormalities in the retina; however, the underlying cause for SARDS is unknown and no treatment exists. We are interested in characterizing this disease better with hopes of identifying protein biomarkers and/or the genetic components of this disease.
current_roster.tagline: Help us understand SARDS better!
current_roster.name: Understanding Sudden Acquired Retinal Degeneration Syndrome in dogs

current_roster.description:
Tears from the ocular surface are drained from the eye through several important structures collectively known as the nasolacrimal apparatus (NLA). This frequently becomes blocked and sometimes infected leading to discomfort, tear staining, eye discharge, and skin inflammation, all of which are associated with a decreased quality of life. Clinically, NLA obstructions can be very frustrating to treat and can often lead to permanent obstruction.

We have established a team at the UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital consisting of specialists with expertise in Ophthalmology, Internal Medicine, Endoscopy, Diagnostic Imaging, and Interventional Radiology and have utilized fluoroscopy to successfully treat NLA obstruction in dogs. We have utilized fluoroscopy, CT, and endoscopy and capitalized on improvements in instrumentation and minimally invasive techniques developed for catheterization of other challenging locations such as the ureters to successfully treat NLA obstruction.

Based upon the success of this initial pilot study, we have initiated a clinical trial to recruit and treat more cases and to evaluate more objective outcome measures.
current_roster.tagline: Help us assess a new treatment that's less invasive for NLA blockages!
current_roster.name: A multi-disciplinary, minimally-invasive treatment for nasolacrimal apparatus (NLA) blockage

current_roster.description: When liver tumors in dogs cannot be removed with surgery, treatment options are limited or non-existent. In humans, one of the standard treatments for those cases is transarterial embolization (TAE), which eliminates the blood supply of the tumor and may decrease tumor size. Therefore, the objectives of this study are to 1) describe the procedure of TAE in a group of dogs with naturally-occurring liver cancer, and 2) evaluate the effect that liver TAE has on clinical signs, size and viability of the tumor.
current_roster.tagline: Help us learn more about this new technique that could shrink liver tumors in dogs!
current_roster.name: Using a new technique to shrink liver tumors in dogs

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to evaluate whether three times weekly dosing with oral rapamycin can reverse the heart muscle changes associated with subvalvular aortic stenosis (SAS) in dogs.  As the current treatment options are limited in this disease, this has the potential to provide further treatment options to improve quantity and quality of life in this disease.
current_roster.name: Assessing an Oral Drug to Reverse Subvalvular Aortic Stenosis (SAS) in Dogs

current_roster.description:
The corneal endothelium is a thin layer of cells at the posterior aspect of the 
cornea responsible for keeping the cornea dehydrated and thus transparent, 
providing clear vision. Corneal endothelial disease can lead to corneal swelling 
(edema), painful corneal blisters (bullous keratopathy) and increased risk of 
postoperative complications after cataract surgeries that may lead to loss of 
vision. Despite advances in cataract surgical techniques, corneal endothelial cell 
damage can occur during the surgery, exacerbating pre-existing endothelial 
disease. Thus, patients with preexisting endothelial disease are at increased risk 
of postoperative complications and it is extremely important to detect low 
corneal endothelial cell density and endothelial disease early.
Early detection of corneal endothelial disease is possible by screening with in 
vivo confocal microscopy (an emerging noninvasive imaging and diagnostic tool) 
and may allow clinicians and owners to make personalized decisions regarding 
close monitoring or institution of therapies to delay disease progression.
current_roster.tagline: Early detection of corneal endothelial disease in dogs
current_roster.name: Help researchers detect early corneal endothelial disease through advanced imaging techniques
current_roster.top_investigator: Bianca Da Costa Martins, DVM, PhD, DACVO

current_roster.description:
Nasal tumors can cause severe nasal bleeding or discharge and difficulty breathing. These tumors often aggressively spread throughout the tissues of the nasal cavity and into the surrounding organs, including the eye and brain. Radiation therapy is the treatment of choice for nasal tumors in dogs; however, radiation therapy isn't often good for long-term control of the tumor. An another treatment option is transarterial embolization, or TAE, which involves the delivery of a mechanical “clot” to the main arteries supplying blood to the tissues of the nasal cavity with the goal of eliminating the blood supply of the tumor and decreasing tumor size.

The purposes of this study are to 1) describe TAE in dogs with naturally-occurring nasal cancer, 2) evaluate the effect that nasal TAE has on the tumor, and 3) evaluate the effect that nasal TAE has on the values measured by positron emission tomography (PET) scanning.
current_roster.tagline: Help us treat nasal tumors in dogs using a new kind of therapy!
current_roster.name: Novel Treatment for Nasal Tumors

current_roster.description: This VMTH clinical trial is investigating the effect of nicotinamide (vitamin B3) given by mouth alone or in combination with a topical drop, ripasudil, that we have previously shown to be effective for the treatment of corneal endothelial disease (CED) in dogs. Dogs with CED have corneal swelling which can decrease their vision. They also can develop corneal ulcers which causes pain and these can become infected. Corneal transplant surgery is the most effective treatment for this disease, but there is limited available donor tissue, and the graft can be rejected. Another surgical option, superficial keratectomy and advancement hood flap (SKAHF), is palliative and does not address the underlying problem. Thus, we need to investigate new medical treatments for CED. We hope that oral nicotinamide alone, or in combination with topical ripasudil, will delay or reverse CED progression.
current_roster.name: Investigating new therapies for dogs with corneal endothelial disease

current_roster.description:
Canine Cutaneous Epitheliotropic T-cell Lymphoma (CETCL) is a rare but aggressive skin cancer in dogs, and sadly, most affected dogs live less than a year after diagnosis, even with chemotherapy. One major reason for this poor prognosis is that we don’t fully understand how the disease develops or progresses, which has made it difficult to create new, effective treatments.

This study aims to change that. By analyzing the microRNA (miRNA) in the skin of dogs with CETCL, we hope to uncover key markers that could help diagnose the disease earlier, predict how it will progress, and track treatment effectiveness. Research in humans with similar cancers has shown that identifying these miRNAs could also lead to the development of new treatment options. Ultimately, our goal is to improve the way we diagnose and care for dogs with CETCL, giving them a better chance for a longer, healthier life.
current_roster.tagline: Looking for dogs with cutaneous lymphoma
current_roster.name: Characterizing Gene Expression in Canine Cutaneous Lymphoma

current_roster.description:
Copper associated liver disease is one of the most common liver diseases in dogs and Labrador retrievers are at risk. Copper associated liver disease is caused by too much copper build up in the liver. If this disease is not diagnosed or treated, it can cause a lot of liver damage and ultimately, liver failure.


The goal of this study is to use new technologies to better understand how to diagnose these diseases with blood tests and see how they differ from Labrador retrievers with autoimmune liver disease and healthy Labrador retrievers.
current_roster.tagline: Looking for Labradors with liver disease and healthy!
current_roster.name: Copper liver disease in Labrador retrievers
current_roster.top_investigator: Tarini Ullal, Asst Professor of Clin Small Animal Int Medicine

current_roster.description:
We are conducting a research study at the UC Davis Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital to understand how a commonly used antibiotic, cefovecin (Convenia®), affects the gut microbiome of healthy cats. While cefovecin is widely prescribed and typically well-tolerated, its long-lasting effects on the intestinal bacteria of cats have never been fully evaluated.


In this study, healthy cats ages 1–10 years will receive a single cefovecin injection, followed by a series of non-invasive fecal sample collections over 16 weeks. These samples will help us evaluate how the gut microbiota changes immediately after treatment and how long it takes to return to normal. We will also analyze whether antibiotics alter important bacterial metabolites and whether any short-term changes in gut health occur.


This research will help veterinarians better understand how antibiotics influence the feline gastrointestinal system and will contribute to improving long-term gut health and antimicrobial stewardship in cats.
current_roster.tagline: Advancing our understanding of feline gut health
current_roster.name: Seeking Healthy Cats for a Gut Microbiome Study
current_roster.top_investigator: Hannah Savage, Assistant Professor of Microbiology

current_roster.description:
Dogs with epilepsy often have normal findings on routine brain imaging, even though seizures are ongoing. This study is evaluating whether a specialized imaging technique called positron emission tomography (PET) can identify areas of abnormal brain activity in dogs with epilepsy.


By identifying functional changes in the brain, PET imaging may help veterinarians better understand seizure disorders, guide treatment decisions, and identify dogs who may benefit from new therapeutic approaches beyond standard anti-seizure medications.
current_roster.tagline: Using PET scans to better understand seizure activity in dogs
current_roster.name: Advanced Brain Imaging for Dogs with Epilepsy

current_roster.description:
High-grade gliomas are aggressive brain tumors that are difficult to treat in dogs. While surgery, radiation therapy, and chemotherapy may help some dogs, we still have much to learn about why some tumors respond better to treatment than others.


The purpose of this study is to better understand brain tumors in dogs by collecting information about each dog's health, MRI findings, tumor characteristics, and in some dogs, how they respond to radiation treatment. By studying many dogs with naturally occurring brain tumors, we hope to identify patterns that will help veterinarians diagnose these tumors more accurately, predict how they may behave, and develop more effective treatments in the future.


Although participation in this study may not directly benefit every dog, the information gained will help improve the care of dogs diagnosed with brain tumors and advance the development of new treatment options. Every dog that participates helps us learn more about brain tumors and brings us one step closer to improving treatment and quality of life for future dogs facing this disease.
current_roster.tagline: A clinical trial to characterize the clinical disease progression in dogs with glioma
current_roster.name: PRISM Trial: Precision Research Integrating Symptoms and Molecular Biology in Canine Glioma
current_roster.top_investigator: Christine Toedebusch, DVM, PhD, DACVIM, Associate Professor

current_roster.description:
Feline hypersomatotropism is an endocrine disorder caused by excessive secretion of growth hormone from a pituitary tumor. This disease can lead to difficult control of diabetes, progressive organ enlargement, cardiac and renal dysfunction, and compression on of the brain by the growing tumor, ultimately causing life-threatening decompensation. To date, the surgical removal of the pituitary tumor, hypophysectomy, is the only treatment that can definitively restore normal hormone levels. 


This study explores how the immune system interacts with pituitary tumors in cats. After removal of the pituitary tumor, we will study the tumor composition and gene activity. We will also explore how immune responses relate to hormone levels, helping us better understand the link between the immune system and hormonal health. Understanding this relationship could help explain how these tumors behave and reveal promising directions for future treatment.
current_roster.tagline: Profiling the immune-endocrine interface in feline hypersomatotropism through hypophysectomy
current_roster.name: Hypophysectomy for cats with Pituitary Tumors

current_roster.description: Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS) or dry eye is a devastating disease that causes ocular pain and potentially blindness. It is seen more frequently in West Highland White Terriers in comparison to many other breeds. We are interested identifying the genetic components of this disease as well as characterizing this disease better through study of the microbiome and testing of the tear film and ocular surface.
current_roster.tagline: Help us find out what genes cause dry eye syndrome (keratoconjunctivitis sicca) in westies!
current_roster.name: Understanding the genes behind dry eye syndrome in West Highland white terriers

current_roster.description: Equine recurrent uveitis (ERU) is the leading cause of blindness in horses, marked by repeated episodes of inflammation of the uveal tract of the eye. Appaloosa horses, known best for their white coat spotting patterns (termed leopard complex or LP), are eight times more likely than any other breed to develop this disease and four times more likely to go blind, suggesting genetics plays a major contributing role. However, little is known about the specific genetic factors involved. The objective of this study is to determine the genetic factors contributing to ERU in multiple horse breeds.
current_roster.tagline: Help us understand why horses get recurrent uveitis!
current_roster.name: Understanding the genetics causing equine recurrent uveitis in horses

current_roster.description: Oculocutaneous Syndrome is associated with the genes responsible for the white spotting in other species. We are interested in characterizing potential ocular abnormalities developing in the white-spotted Italian Greyhound dogs and identify the genetic mutations.
current_roster.name: Oculocutaneous Syndrome in Italian Greyhounds With White Spotting

current_roster.description:
Sebaceous adenitis is a skin disease caused by inflammation and eventual destruction of the sebaceous glands. The sebaceous glands are located next to the hair follicle (‘hair bed’). 
A generalized form occurs with large amounts of scale (‘dandruff’) on the skin, scale adherent to hairs and skin often dry to the touch.  As the disease progresses (often from the face or head toward the tail), there is a generalized thinning of the coat. The cause is not completely understood, but several breeds have been shown to have a higher incidence of this disease, including the Akita, thus genetics seems to play a part. Diagnosis is by clinical appearance as well as skin biopsy, which shows under the microscope either inflammation of the sebaceous glands, or a lack of sebaceous glands in the skin.

The purpose of this study is to determine if there is a difference in the DNA of Akitas with the disease sebaceous adenitis and those without the disease. There will be about 8 pets taking part in this study.  
We invite your pet to take part in this clinical trial because your dog can serve either as one of the dogs with the disease, or as a control dog if it does not have the disease. Pets that are not in a study are usually treated by certain medicated shampoos, cyclosporine, and/or retinoids. Being in this study will not affect or change any treatment the dog is currently being given.
current_roster.tagline: Help us learn more about this skin disease in Akitas!
current_roster.name: Evaluating the genetic differences in Akita dogs with and without sebaceous adenitis

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to prospectively evaluate the response of nasal cancer to a combination of therapies (chemotherapy and radiation therapy) in dogs.
current_roster.tagline: Help us find new treatments for dogs with nasal cancer!
current_roster.name: Using a combination of therapies for treatment of nasal cancer in dogs

current_roster.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the outcomes for dogs treated palliatively with standard amputation (no chemotherapy). Recent data indicates that at least 35% of dogs do not appear to benefit from standard chemotherapy for this disease. To better understand whether chemotherapy is truly beneficial, this trial aims to document the outcomes prospectively and accurately for dogs whose owners have elected to treat only with surgery (amputation).

There will be about 120 dogs taking part in this study across North America. Study sites include UC Davis, Purdue University, University of Wisconsin, Madison, Tufts University and Ohio State University.
current_roster.tagline: Help us understand how osteosarcoma affects dogs!
current_roster.name: Characterization of naturally occurring osteosarcoma in dogs

current_roster.description: The purpose of this study is to try and improve pain control in dogs with arthritis by evaluating the blood supply to arthritic joints and pursuing a novel therapy, namely vessel embolization.
current_roster.tagline: Help us learn about a new treatment for arthritis pain in dogs!
current_roster.name: Assessment of the blood supply to dog joints with arthritis and evaluation of a new technique for pain control

current_roster.description: The study compares the impact of an individually tailored MEMO plan to a standard generalized treatment plan for managing FIC symptoms and aims to identify the changes in novel blood stress biomarkers called the CTRA . Results could help improve care and outcomes for cats with chronic lower urinary tract signs.
current_roster.tagline: Reducing stress, improving health: Advancing care for cats with FIC
current_roster.name: Exploring Stress Reduction Strategies for Cats with Feline Interstitial Cystitis (FIC): A Study on Environmental Enrichment Therapy and Biomarkers

current_roster.description:
Congenital liver diseases in dogs are diseases present from birth. Examples include portal vein hypoplasia (small to absent portal veins in the liver) or ductal plate malformations (abnormal bile ducts). The purpose of this study is to describe how dogs present with these diseases and how their disease changes over their lifetime. This study is important because there are no long-term studies in dogs with these diseases so clinical course and outcomes are not known and there are no guidelines for treatment and management.


After diagnosis, blood work, urine, stool testing will be performed at 6 months, 12 months, and then yearly thereafter and will be covered as part of the study. This is an observational study so treatment is not dictated. Rather, this is a study evaluating clinical, bloodwork parameters, and overall long-term outcomes in dogs with these conditions. This is a study in collaboration with Colorado State University.
current_roster.tagline: Studying how liver diseases from birth affects health over a lifetime in dogs
current_roster.name: Portal vein hypoplasia and ductal plate malformation (blood vessel/bile duct diseases) of the liver in dogs
current_roster.top_investigator: Tarini Ullal, Asst Professor of Clin Small Animal Int Medicine

current_roster.description: Canine Degenerative Myelopathy (DM) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease of dogs with no known treatments. Diagnosis of this disease is currently not possible prior to death, as it requires examination of the spinal cord under a microscope. This clinical trial is being done to test a new way to diagnose DM in dogs while they are still living, using blood and/or spinal fluid. The development of a diagnostic test before death will help us guide owner decision-making and potentially identify dogs early in their disease process for future clinical trials testing new treatments.
current_roster.tagline: Help us improve diagnosis of Degenerative Myelopathy by enrolling your dog in our study
current_roster.name: Using Spinal Fluid to Help Diagnose Degenerative Myelopathy (DM)
current_roster.top_investigator: Christine Toedebusch, DVM, PhD, Assistant Professor

current_roster.description: This is an observational study, meaning that no treatments or medications are given as part of the research. We are simply collecting a small blood sample from dogs with pemphigus foliaceus to study how certain genes behave in the bloodstream. This information may help researchers better understand why this autoimmune skin disease develops and how it might be diagnosed or treated in the future.
current_roster.tagline: Advancing care for dogs with autoimmune skin disease
current_roster.name: Uncovering the Genetic Clues Behind Pemphigus Foliaceous

current_roster.description:
Corneal endothelial dystrophy (CED) is a devastating disease in dogs that can result in blindness and severe ocular pain from secondary complications. The endothelial cells comprise the most inner aspect of the cornea and are responsible for maintaining a proper fluid balance. This function is critical to ensuring that the cornea remains transparent for vision. In many animals, including dogs, corneal endothelial cells have a very limited capacity to regenerate following injury. In canine patients with CED, the endothelial cells degenerate until the cells still remaining can no longer function properly. This results in swelling of the cornea (edema) which results in decreased vision as well as formation of small fluid-filled blisters (bullae) on the cornea which can rupture and cause ocular discomfort. There are palliative treatments such as hypertonic saline to decrease corneal bullae formation but the only definitive treatment for this condition is a corneal transplant (penetrating keratoplasty). Unfortunately, corneal transplants are rarely performed in canine patients with CED due to the expense of the surgery and follow-up care, relatively high risk of complications, and lack of appropriate donor tissue.


Several dog breeds, including Boxers are seen more commonly for CED in comparison to other breeds. This observation suggests that this disease may have a genetic component. A similar condition called Fuch’s endothelial corneal dystrophy (FECD) exists in humans and several genes associated with FECD have been identified. We propose to identify the region of the dog genome associated with CED in various canine breeds. In order to do this, we will perform thorough eye examinations and use non-invasive advanced imaging techniques to examine various canine breeds including Boxers with CED and age-matched control dogs. We will collect blood from these dogs to obtain DNA. The entire canine genome will be evaluated for an association with CED. This work will be used to identify the gene(s) responsible for this condition in various canine breeds including Boxers. The ultimate goal will be to develop a genetic test for CED in Boxers.
current_roster.name: Understanding Corneal Endothelial Dystrophy in Boxers
current_roster.top_investigator: Sara M. Thomasy DVM, PhD, DACVO, Principal Investigator

current_roster.description:
For dogs diagnosed with oral cancer (Squamous Cell Carcinoma, Oral Malignant Melanoma), curative intent surgical removal has been consistently found to have the longest remission rate. However, conventional diagnostic imaging, which we use to plan our surgery, is imperfect and can underestimate the extent of the tumor which results in the potential that not all cancer cells are removed during surgery. This directly impacts patient outcomes (disease free interval and overall survival). There is a critical need to improve our ability to detect cancer intraoperatively (i.e. during the surgery) to improve patient outcomes.


Further, for human head and neck cancer the standard of care is to give immunotherapy (drugs that improve the immune system's ability to fight off cancer) prior to surgery, which has resulted in increased survival in a subset of patients. We have no data on this type of pre-surgical treatment in dogs, and if it would also improve patient survival times.


The purpose of this study is to evaluate the use of a theranostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) before surgery to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer. This agent is an immunotherapeutic drug (anti-PDL1) bound to a fluorophore. This drug would be given 2X before treatment (surgery or other).


Through this study we will determine if this drug can allow us to see residual cancer cells during surgery (differentiate cancer from healthy tissue) and if treatment of the tumor before surgery with the drug can improve the local anti-tumor immune response (decreased in percent viable cells in the tumor).


If successful this could overall vastly improve our ability to treat oral cancer in dogs.
current_roster.tagline: New theragnostic agent (diagnostic and therapeutic) to improve our ability to effectively treat oral cancer!
current_roster.name: Fluorescence Imaging with PDL1-IRDye800 to Guide Surgical Treatment of Oral Cancer in Dogs
current_roster.top_investigator: Stephanie Goldschmidt, BVM&S, DAVDC, DEVDC, F-OMFS, Associate Professor, Dentistry and Oral Surgery

current_roster.description:
​Canine chronic enteropathy (CE) is long-term disorder of the intestinal tract in dogs, causing symptoms such as decreased appetite, vomiting, and diarrhea that significantly impact both affected dogs and their caregivers. CE is not fully understood, but may result from a complex interaction of genetics, environmental factors, changes in the gut microbiome, and an abnormal immune response.  

Current treatment strategies aim to restore intestinal balance by targeting these contributing factors. This includes altering the gut microbiota through dietary interventions, prebiotics and probiotics, and regulating  the immune system via immunomodulatory or immunosuppressive therapies. 

N-acetyl-glucosamine (NAG) is a naturally occurring amino sugar that has shown promise in reducing intestinal inflammation in both human and rat models of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Its mechanism of action is thought to involve enhancement of short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, which plays a critical role in maintaining intestinal barrier integrity and regulating immune responses. 

This study aims to investigate the potential therapeutic effects of NAG in dogs diagnosed with CE. By evaluating clinical symptoms, inflammatory markers, and microbiome composition, we aim to determine whether NAG can serve as a beneficial additional treatment for managing canine CE. ​
current_roster.tagline: A clinical trial to investigate the effects of NAG on gut health and quality of life in dogs with chronic enteropathy
current_roster.name: Investigating the effects of N-acetyl-glucosamine (NAG) in dogs with chronic enteropathy (CE)

L40: # Ongoing EU Clinical Trials
L41: ESVONC attaches great importance to innovation and evidence-based medicine in the field of veterinary oncology. Therefore, we are happy to share with you with a monthly overview of ongoing canine and feline oncology trials in Europe. We are convinced that knowledge of these trials will enhance collaboration between researchers and clinicians, thus increasing recruitment for clinical trials and treatment options for dogs and cats.
L42: Please find below a non-exhaustive listing of ongoing trials as gathered in the Oncowaf database. For more details about these trials, please visit 【39†https://oncowaf.be/en/ClinicalTrials†oncowaf.be】.
L43: If you have an ongoing clinical trial and would like to add it to the Oncowaf clinical trial database and this mailing, please contact contact@oncowaf.com. This list is an intiative of dr. Laetitia Cicchelero (DVM, PhD, Cross-health coordinator @ Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Ghent University). Laetitia is initiator and inspirer of ONCOWAF. ESVONC wishes to thank Laetitia for her efforts to create this useful overview.
L44: This list is updated on a monthly basis.
